title: Fault Tolerance & Redundancy Models
intro: Fault-tolerant systems anticipate, absorb, and recover from hardware crashes, network severed links, and software bugs without total system collapse.
objectives: Classify failure modes: Crash-Stop, Crash-Recovery, and Byzantine Faults.
Implement N+2 redundancy, active-passive vs active-active failovers.
Apply the Bulkhead pattern to prevent single component failures from consuming all resources.
body:
### Core Redundancy Models
- **Active-Passive (Warm/Cold Standby)**: Primary node handles 100% of traffic; secondary replica syncs data and takes over only when primary fails via heartbeat heartbeat fencing. May incur 10-60s failover downtime.
- **Active-Active (Multi-Master)**: All nodes concurrently serve read and write traffic across multiple availability zones. Requires distributed conflict resolution.
- **N+2 Redundancy**: System provisions $N$ nodes required for peak traffic plus 2 additional spare nodes to absorb simultaneous node failures and rolling OS upgrades without capacity degradation.
keyIdea: Design for failure as a constant reality. Isolate resources with bulkheads and provision N+2 headroom so node crashes cause zero customer degradation.

concepts.title: Bulkhead Isolation
concepts.body: Partitioning thread pools, connection pools, and memory so a crash or delay in a non-essential service (e.g. recommendations) cannot freeze checkout processing.

concepts.title: Graceful Degradation
concepts.body: Automatically disabling heavy non-essential features (personalized widgets, animations) to keep core transaction paths responsive during outages.

examples: Netflix Chaos Monkey randomly killing production AWS instances to enforce fault resilience.

quiz.prompt: What does the Bulkhead pattern accomplish in distributed microservices?
options: Isolates critical resource pools so failure in one subsystem does not consume all resources and crash the host process
quiz.explanation: Like compartments in a ship's hull, bulkheads isolate failures and prevent total process collapse.
